# Satya Nadella Says Renting AI Capacity to a Few Big Customers Is “Not a Business”

Satya Nadella drew a sharp line between the AI customers Microsoft wants and the ones it will tolerate, and the distinction reveals something uncomfortable about how the biggest names in cloud infrastructure actually make their money.

![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/dac1a1f2adf30aac00a449ddbb2a0950?s=44&d=mm&r=g)

By [Omor Ibne Ehsan](https://247wallst.com/author/omor-ibne-ehsan/)

Published October 29, 2026, 8:46am ET · 3 min read

[𝕏](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2F247wallst.com%2Finvesting%2F2026%2F10%2F29%2Fsatya-nadella-says-renting-ai-capacity-to-a-few-big-customers-is-not-a-business%2F&text=Satya%20Nadella%20Says%20Renting%20AI%20Capacity%20to%20a%20Few%20Big%20Customers%20Is%20%E2%80%9CNot%20a%20Business%E2%80%9D) [f](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2F247wallst.com%2Finvesting%2F2026%2F10%2F29%2Fsatya-nadella-says-renting-ai-capacity-to-a-few-big-customers-is-not-a-business%2F)

 ![Satya Nadella Says Renting AI Capacity to a Few Big Customers Is “Not a Business”](https://247wallst.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/imageforentry202.jpg) 

© Justin Sullivan / Getty Images

 

On the September-quarter earnings call of **Microsoft** ([NASDAQ:MSFT](https://247wallst.com/companies/MSFT/) | [MSFT Price Prediction](https://247wallst.com/companies/msft/price-prediction)), held October 28, 2026, Satya Nadella compared the enterprise customers he wants with “like 4 customers who buy a lot of capacity from you and you can show a few quarters of growth.” He added, “And that’s not a business as far as I’m concerned.”

The remark came from results in which Microsoft reported revenue of $92.3 billion, up 19%, with Azure revenue up 48%. Shares closed at $531.01 before the release, down 0.06%, leaving the company worth $3.94 trillion. After the call, they traded at $546.39 at about 7:59 p.m. ET, up 2.90%.

## Nadella’s Remark Is About Pricing Discipline

A Bernstein Research analyst asked how much of Azure’s AI demand comes from enterprises. Satya Nadella said Rolls-Royce runs jet-engine maintenance across 30,000 parts on Foundry, Microsoft’s platform for building AI agents, and that Austrian bank RBI showed him 20-plus business processes end to end.

These are recurring workflows that use compute every day, so they last longer than a one-time capacity purchase. Nadella did not name any company. He said Microsoft is “open for business” with large buyers because “as long as the pricing is right, we may sell them some.”

## One Pool of Capacity in a Supply Shortage

Nadella told Morgan Stanley’s Adam Wood that “we have one pool and we want to get the pool to be as efficient and fungible.” Fungible capacity is hardware that can shift among many customers and workloads, which lowers the risk that one departing buyer leaves expensive chips idle.

Amy Hood said capex of $45.2 billion came in below her July 29 guide of over $50 billion “as some third-party capacity deliveries we expected in Q1 were delayed.” She added that “Customer demand continues to exceed available supply.”

For the December quarter, Amy Hood guided Azure growth of 49% to 50% in constant currency and capex of over $50 billion, with calendar-year spending of approximately $170 billion. A company that is short on supply can afford to be choosy on price, so the stance costs Microsoft little.

## Microsoft Carries Its Own Big-Customer Exposure

Commercial remaining performance obligation, which is contracted revenue not yet recognized, rose 73% to $677 billion, while commercial bookings fell 12%. Hood tied the decline to “large Azure commitments in the prior year,” partly offset by “a large Azure commitment this quarter.”

Microsoft also recorded $10.0 billion of revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI out of $92.279 billion, or about 10.8%. It also buys third-party capacity, so it sits on both sides of the model Nadella questioned.

For comparison, **CoreWeave** ([NASDAQ:CRWV](https://247wallst.com/companies/CRWV/)) closed at $63.93 on October 28. For the June 2026 quarter, it reported three unnamed customers at 36%, 26% and 10% of revenue. **Oracle** ([NYSE:ORCL](https://247wallst.com/companies/ORCL/)) closed at $144.54 with $638 billion of remaining performance obligations. S&P Global Ratings (SGR) estimates OpenAI accounts for roughly half of that total.

## What Investors Should Track in Microsoft’s Next Report

Microsoft’s results support its growth case. Demand is running ahead of supply, so capacity is what limits revenue, and the growing backlog shows customers are signing commitments years in advance.

The risks are heavy capex, delayed third-party deliveries, and the share of revenue that comes from OpenAI. Spreading AI across many enterprise workflows is how Microsoft reduces that concentration over time, and this quarter showed that spread growing.

All of that capex has to be powered and cooled by somebody, which is why the suppliers behind the data centers keep showing up alongside the hyperscalers themselves. We pulled together seven of them in a [free report on the AI infrastructure buildout](https://247wallst.com/pages/ai-power-seven-offer-d905ec99.html).

Microsoft has not confirmed the date of its next report. If Azure growth falls short of Amy Hood’s 49% to 50% guidance, or OpenAI’s share of revenue rises above about 10.8%, the case for breadth gets weaker.

**OPERATOR**

Greetings and welcome to the Microsoft Fiscal Year 2027 First Quarter Earnings Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. A question-and-answer session will follow the formal presentation. If anyone should require operator assistance, please press star zero on your telephone keypad. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. It is now my pleasure to introduce Jonathan Nielsen, Vice President of Investor Relations.

**Jonathan Nielsen (Vice President of Investor Relations)**

Good afternoon and thank you for joining us today. On the call Satya Nadella, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, Amy Hood, Chief Financial Officer, Alice Joller, Chief Accounting Officer, and Brian Defoe, Deputy General Counsel and Corporate Secretary. On the Microsoft Investor Relations site you can find our earnings press release and Financial Summary Slide Deck, which is intended to supplement our prepared remarks during today’s call and provides the reconciliation of differences between GAAP and non-GAAP financial measures.

More detailed Outlook slides will be available on the Microsoft Investor Relations website when we provide Outlook commentary on today’s call. On this call we will discuss certain non-GAAP items. The non-GAAP financial measures provided should not be considered a substitute for or superior to the measures of financial performance prepared in accordance with GAAP. They are included as additional clarifying items to aid investors in further understanding the company’s first quarter performance. In addition to the impact these items and events have on the financial results, all growth comparisons we make on the call today relate to the corresponding period of last year unless otherwise noted.

We will also provide growth rates in constant currency when available, as a framework for assessing how underlying business performed excluding the effect of foreign currency rate valuations. Where growth rates are in constant currency, we will refer to the growth rate only. We’ll post our prepared remarks to our website immediately following the call until the complete transcript is available. Today’s call is being webcast live and recorded. If you ask a question, it will be included in our live transmission, in the transcript and in any future use of the recording.

You can replay the call and view the transcript on the Microsoft Investor Relations website. During this call we will be making forward-looking statements which are predictions, projections or other statements about future events. These statements are based on current expectations and assumptions that are subject to risks and uncertainties. Actual results could materially differ because of factors discussed in today’s earnings press release, in the comments made during this conference call, and the Risk Factors section of our Form 10-K, Forms 10-Q and other reports and filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

We do not undertake any duty to update any forward-looking statement and with that I’ll turn the call over to Satya.

**Satya Nadella (Chairman and Chief Executive Officer)**

Thank you very much, Jonathan. It was a fast start to our fiscal year. Microsoft Cloud revenue surpassed $63 billion with growth accelerating to 30% year over year. We are focused on three things: designing AI to empower people, ensuring every organization has sovereignty over its own learning, and building trust with controls that ensure agent safety and security. Now let’s talk about how we are making progress on those goals as we build a new tech stack, starting with Copilot. We announced our biggest update to Copilot to date this quarter, bringing together chat, cowork, autopilot, and code into one unified experience. It’s one product experience across commercial and consumer and comes with all of Office built in. We think of Copilot as the new OS for work. Customers are increasingly turning to Copilot to get real work done.

Automated tasks have nearly doubled since July. Daily users are up nearly 50% quarter over quarter and over 5x year over year. User satisfaction improved nearly 20% quarter over quarter to another all-time high. And 90% of Copilot queries use Auto Mode, which dynamically routes tasks across models, optimizing for quality, speed, and cost. These improvements are translating into larger purchases. The number of customers with more than 50,000 Copilot seats increased over 8x year over year, including Capital, Gemini, HCLTech, Hitachi, Tris Financial, and the UK Revenue and Customs Department.

And just last week, Volkswagen announced plans to deploy Copilot to more than 330,000 employees, one of the largest deployments to date in Europe. We’re also seeing strong momentum with E7, which brings together Copilot, E5, Entra, and Agent 365. Thousands of customers in every industry have purchased the suite to date, including Amadeus, BlackRock, Fiserv, New South Wales Health Department, and Zeiss. Our business model is expanding from per-seat subscriptions to include consumption, expanding our TAM and ARPU.

The subscription brings increasingly capable everyday intelligence to every user, typically IT-funded, consolidating frontier advances for everyone across the organization, and as agents take on higher-value work, consumption opens up business-funded demand with spending tied directly to the value these agents deliver. The number of Copilot customers actively consuming credits through usage-based billing grew over 75% over the quarter. When it comes to software development, all major coding agents have shown up to work on GitHub. Agent-generated PRs have increased 6x over the past six months, and agents now open more than a third of all PRs on the platform. We are very hard at work on reliability as agentic activity on GitHub. At Universe this morning, we shared how we are expanding capacity and rebuilding the core Git architecture. Also at Universe, we announced broad availability of Copilot Fusion, which is all about bringing multi-model orchestration to software development.

It delivers frontier-level quality up to 40% faster and at up to 77% lower cost. Credit consumption from agentic features on GitHub has more than doubled since usage-based billing went into effect, and we’re also helping developers secure their code and turn AI-generated code into high-quality software. GitHub Advanced Security revenue increased over 50% year over year as customers use its AI capabilities to scan entire repos and fix vulnerabilities in real time.

In the business application space, we are extending this vision of Copilot as the new OS for work, bringing the business logic and capabilities of Dynamics 365 directly into Copilot and helping every organization stand up their own infinite SaaS factory. This quarter, we introduced new Copilot skills across Dynamics 365, which enable customers to access CRM and ERP capabilities directly in the flow of work. In recruiting, more than 10 million members use our LinkedIn AI-powered job search daily, and 25,000 customers are using our AgentIQ hiring solutions. Recruiters using Hiring Assistant are finding interview-quality applicants 33% faster while reviewing 83% fewer profiles to find a qualified match.

In healthcare, we automated million patient encounters this quarter, up 70% year over year, helping clinicians spend less time on administrative work and more time with patients. Ten providers, including Advocate Health, Mass General Brigham, Mercy, Intermountain Health, and others, have used our solutions to document over 1 million encounters each since the beginning of the calendar year. And in science, our teams are working with customers to use Discovery to accelerate scientific process. A great example is Saint-Gobain, which used Discovery to accelerate the development of low-carbon construction materials.

Underneath our first-party agentic experiences is a common platform. It starts with Foundry, which is becoming an increasingly important driver of our growth. Foundry helps organizations build learning loops grounded in their business context and deploy agents safely at scale. We now have over 120,000 Foundry customers, with revenue more than tripling year over year. Foundry’s model choice and feature set, coupled with its deep integration across our stack, is driving differentiation.

Azure OpenAI directly benefited in the last quarter with big advances in OpenAI models, and when you couple this with our model choice built into Foundry, customers are able to build solutions optimizing across quality, cost, performance. In fact, the number of customers building agentic solutions with multiple models increased 5x year over year, and revenue from open-source models on Foundry increased 10x. We also continue to make rapid progress with our first-party models. Our goal is to advance the cost-to-outcome frontier, which means delivering capabilities comparable to leading models within three to six months of their release at a fraction of the training cost, thereby allowing us to transfer those cost benefits to customers, and you see this in our products today. MAI Cyber now powers over 40% of the scans in our code scanner at 18% lower cost per scan.

MAI Transcribe is the most accurate and cheapest transcription model in the world, supporting Dragon Copilot’s multilingual workflow. MAI Code Flash had 3 million users in GitHub Copilot last month alone, helping developers get more out of their AI credits. Microsoft Decision One is our new model for structured decision making, outperforming both LLMs and other decision models in latency and quality. Over 4,000 customers, including Atos, Equinor, and RBI, have already used it in the first months since its release.

And we recently completed pre-training MAI Base 2, which outperforms other open-weight models we tested with 4 to 12 times greater training compute efficiency. This base model will be used in upcoming MAI models across Thinking, Code, and Cyber. Beyond models, we are making the harness behind our own Copilot experiences available to customers in Foundry. It gives customers a Microsoft-managed way to build agents that reason, use tools, complete complex, long-running work, while preserving their choice of model.

Another critical layer is data. We now have 44,000 paid Fabric customers, up more than 50% year over year. We are bringing Foundry and Fabric closer together so you can build your own agents right next to data. Over 19,000 customers now use Foundry and Fabric as enterprises connect and operate agents over real-time operational, analytical, and unstructured data. Customers are also rapidly deploying our AI-optimized databases, including PostgreSQL, SQL DB Hyperscale, and Cosmos DB, to give agents fast, secure access to the data and context they need.

PostgreSQL growth accelerated for the fourth consecutive quarter, and the number of PostgreSQL customers also using Foundry accelerated to 90% year over year. We also have one of the most important databases for any enterprise, which is the knowledge underneath Microsoft 365, spanning people, their relationships, documents, emails, meetings, chats, projects, and other artifacts. WorkIQ makes this context available to every agentic workload, and with Microsoft IQ, we’re bringing together WorkIQ, Fabric IQ, and Foundry IQ—a unified context for agentic systems.

Nearly 60,000 customers are accessing context across Microsoft IQ, up 25% quarter over quarter. As enterprises deploy more agents, they also need to govern them at scale. With Agent 365, we provide a platform for AI observability, enabling customers to manage, secure, and optimize the performance and cost of their agents. Over 50 million agents are now in the registry, up over 30% quarter over quarter. And finally, as agents gain greater access to enterprise data and systems, security becomes even more critical. Our approach is to separate intelligence from authority, enforcing entity permissions, monitoring, and containment outside the model itself.

Last week, we expanded Perception with new capabilities to help customers secure and contain agentic insiders, including expanded agent discovery across local and cloud environments, dynamic permissions that enforce least-privileged access for each task, and continuous risk assessment. We also introduced teams of Guardian agents that continuously monitor agent activity to help prevent unsafe actions before they occur. And we are seeing encouraging feedback on Perception overall from preview customers including KPMG, Nationwide Building Society, Northern Trust, and Cellentis.

More broadly, we are helping custom

# Microsoft's search and ad sales, now with LinkedIn, gain 10% to $6.6bn

Bing advertisers lose their search-only figure: ex-TAC growth of 12% now blends in LinkedIn ads. December guidance calls for low-double-digit growth again.

* [![Luis Rijo](/content/images/size/w2000/2024/09/rijo.webp)](/author/luis/)  by [Luis Rijo](https://ppc.land/author/luis/)

Microsoft reported on October 28, 2026 that revenue from its **Search and advertising** business rose 10% to $6.55bn in the three months to September 30, the first quarter in which that line combines LinkedIn's advertising and Premium subscription businesses with Bing, Microsoft Edge and MSN. The new grouping, one of several introduced with a two-segment structure Microsoft announced in September, means the company no longer publishes a growth rate for search advertising on its own.

The rest of the quarter was dominated by infrastructure. Total revenue reached $92.3bn, up 19%, and operating income climbed 21% to $45.9bn, according to the earnings release. Azure revenue grew 48%. Capital expenditures, including finance leases, came to $45.2bn, and the 10-Q filed the same day shows $364.6bn of datacenter and other leases signed but not yet started. The filing also shows that commercial arrangements with OpenAI produced $10.0bn of revenue in the quarter, close to 11% of the company's sales.

## In Short

Microsoft earned more from ads between July and September than a year before, but it now adds LinkedIn's ads and paid memberships to the same pile as Bing, so the 10% rise cannot be lined up against the Bing numbers it used to publish. That matters to anyone who buys ads on Bing or LinkedIn, because the company has stopped saying how fast search ads alone are growing. Microsoft expects growth in the low double digits again for October to December, while it keeps spending more than $45bn a quarter on data centers and chips.

## A new line for advertisers to read

Until June, Microsoft reported search revenue under a metric it called search and news advertising, later shortened to search advertising, and tracked LinkedIn as a separate business. That ended with fiscal 2027. According to the 10-Q, Microsoft in September 2026 "announced changes in our segment reporting structure," creating an **Agents and Infra** segment that "brings together our applications and agents, our multi-model system, and Azure infrastructure," and a **Devices and Consumer** segment covering its consumer products.

The search line moved with it. In the 10-Q, the Search and advertising product line now covers "Bing, Microsoft Edge, LinkedIn Marketing Solutions and Premium Subscriptions, third-party affiliates, and MSN." The investor metric that matters most to search marketers, revenue excluding traffic acquisition costs, has been redefined in the same way. It now measures revenue "from search advertising excluding traffic acquisition costs" paid to Bing Ads network publishers and content partners, "as well as revenue from LinkedIn Marketing Solutions (ex TAC) and Premium Subscriptions," according to the filing.

LinkedIn itself has been divided. Its Talent Solutions and Sales Solutions businesses now sit inside a new Industry solutions cloud metric, alongside Dynamics 365 and Healthcare and Life Sciences cloud, in the Agents and Infra segment. Its advertising and consumer subscription revenue sits in Devices and Consumer. LinkedIn as a whole no longer has a reported revenue figure.

The effect on the numbers is large. Under the old definition, Microsoft's [fiscal 2026 search advertising revenue was $15.18bn](https://ppc.land/microsoft-search-ad-growth-drops-to-10-as-azure-tops-100-billion/), up from $13.88bn the year before. The recast Search and advertising line in Microsoft's financial statements puts fiscal 2026 at $24.84bn. The difference, $9.66bn by PPC Land's calculation, approximates what moved into the line. Microsoft does not break it down.

Growth rates shift too. Microsoft's spreadsheets restate the last four quarters on the new basis, in both reported and [constant currency](https://ppc.land/constant-currency/) terms, and in three of them the new metric runs higher than the figure first reported.

| Quarter | Ex-TAC growth as first reported (old search metric) | Ex-TAC growth recast (new Search and advertising, GAAP / constant currency) | Search and advertising revenue, recast ($m) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Q1 FY26 (to Sept 2025) | 16% | 16% / 15% | 5,942 |
| Q2 FY26 (to Dec 2025) | 10% | 13% / 12% | 6,393 |
| Q3 FY26 (to Mar 2026) | 12% | 14% / 11% | 6,065 |
| Q4 FY26 (to June 2026) | 10% | 13% / 12% | 6,435 |
| Q1 FY27 (to Sept 2026) | not published | 12% / 12% | 6,554 |

The first-reported figures come from PPC Land's coverage of each quarter: [16% in the September 2025 quarter](https://ppc.land/microsoft-cloud-revenue-hits-49-1-billion-as-ai-investments-accelerate/), [10% in December](https://ppc.land/microsofts-search-ad-growth-slows-to-10/), [12% in March](https://ppc.land/microsoft-search-ads-bounce-back-to-12-as-ai-business-hits-37b-run-rate/) and 10% in June. On the recast basis, the June quarter grew 13% rather than 10%. Read against the old series, the 12% reported on October 28 looks like an acceleration. Read against the new series, it is a one-point slowdown from June and, on a reported basis, the weakest rate in the five quarters shown.

## What drove the 12%

Amy Hood, Microsoft's chief financial officer, gave the explanation in one sentence on the call. "Search advertising revenue ex-TAC increased 12% and was ahead of expectations driven by higher volume and rate across LinkedIn, Edge, and Bing," she said. The 10-Q gives the same explanation.

In Microsoft's usage, rate refers broadly to pricing and volume to the amount of advertising sold. The company gave no figures for either, and it did not say how the gain split between LinkedIn, Edge and Bing.

Satya Nadella, chairman and chief executive, added a share claim without numbers. "In search and advertising, Bing and Edge once again took share," he said. On LinkedIn he offered an engagement measure instead of a revenue one: "In LinkedIn, engagement continues to deepen across our more than 1.4 billion members, with time spent viewing content in the Feed up over 15 percent year over year."

The gap between the two growth rates is telling. Total Search and advertising revenue rose 10.3%, from $5,942m to $6,554m, while the ex-TAC measure rose 12%. Traffic acquisition costs therefore grew more slowly than revenue, or fell. Microsoft does not disclose the TAC amount. In July, PPC Land reported that Microsoft had guided the September quarter's search growth to the [mid-single digits, down sequentially, citing third-party partnerships](https://ppc.land/microsoft-search-ad-growth-drops-to-10-as-azure-tops-100-billion/). That forecast was made on the old, Bing-centered metric, and with that metric gone there is no way to check it against the result.

In dollars, the line added $119m on the June quarter, a 1.8% sequential increase. It accounted for 7.1% of Microsoft's revenue, down from 7.7% a year earlier, as Azure grew far faster. Within Devices and Consumer, though, Search and advertising is now the largest business. It generated 42% of the segment's $15.48bn of revenue, ahead of Xbox at $5.38bn and Windows OEM and devices at $3.55bn.

For the December quarter, Hood said: "Search advertising revenue ex-TAC growth should be in the low-double digits driven by consistent trends in rate and volume, with overall search and advertising revenue expected to grow at a similar rate." On a recast base of $6.39bn, growth of 10% or more would put the line above $7bn in a single quarter for the first time, by PPC Land's calculation.

## The quarter in numbers

The headline figures beat the guidance Microsoft gave in July, when it forecast [revenue of $89.85bn to $90.95bn](https://ppc.land/microsoft-search-ad-growth-drops-to-10-as-azure-tops-100-billion/). Revenue came in at $92.28bn, $1.33bn above the top of that range. The comparisons below are year on year.

* Revenue: $92.28bn, up 19%, from $77.67bn
* Gross margin: $62.56bn, up 17%; gross margin percentage 68%, down one point
* Operating expenses: $16.64bn, up 6%
* Operating income: $45.92bn, up 21% (22% in constant currency); operating margin 50%, against 49%
* Net income: $36.63bn, up 32% on a GAAP basis; $36.42bn, up 18%, excluding the impact of OpenAI investments
* Diluted earnings per share: $4.92, up 32%; $4.89, up 18%, on the same adjusted basis
* Effective tax rate: 20%, against 19%

"We delivered a strong start to the fiscal year with Microsoft Cloud revenue of $63.9 billion, with growth accelerating to 30% (up 31% in constant currency) year-over-year," Hood said in the release. "Results exceeded expectations across revenue, operating income, and earnings per share."

Nadella's statement in the release focused on product positioning. "We are delivering greater capability, choice, control, and cost efficiency for customers across our entire stack," he said. "By helping organizations build and own their own intelligence, and earning trust through agent safety and security, we are translating our innovation into growing adoption and real-world impact across every industry."

### Agents and Infra

The new commercial segment produced $76.80bn of revenue, up 25%, and $40.56bn of operating income, up 24%. Its operating margin slipped to 52.8% from 53.1%, by PPC Land's calculation, which Microsoft attributed to "sales mix shift to Azure," a lower-margin business than software subscriptions. Cost of revenue in the segment jumped 35%, driven by "investments in datacenter infrastructure," according to the earnings slides.

Azure revenue reached $33.17bn, up $10.78bn or 48%. Azure on its own was five times the size of Search and advertising, and its year-on-year increase alone exceeded the whole advertising line. In July Microsoft had guided to Azure growth of about 45% in constant currency, though the Azure metric was also redefined for fiscal 2027 "for the movement of certain components," according to the 10-Q, so the two numbers are not on an identical basis.

Hood attributed the beat to Foundry, Microsoft's platform for building AI applications and agents, and to squeezing more out of existing hardware. "Azure revenue was ahead of expectations and increased 48%, even with the 3P capacity delays noted earlier, driven by Foundry and improved CPU monetization," she said. Pricing helped as well. "We had higher token pricing than we expected in the quarter," Hood told analysts, referring to the [tokens](https://ppc.land/tokens/) that AI models consume and that cloud customers pay for.

Other lines in the segment:

* Microsoft 365 cloud: $27.78bn, up 17%. Commercial cloud revenue rose 17% reported and 18% adjusted for a one-point prior-year benefit. Paid commercial seats, which now include paid GitHub seats, grew 5%.
* Microsoft 365 consumer cloud: up 17%, with subscribers up 7%, slowing as Microsoft laps a price increase from the prior year.
* Productivity and server licensing: $8.41bn, down 3%.
* Industry solutions: $5.34bn, up 9%; Industry solutions cloud, which includes LinkedIn Talent and Sales Solutions, up 10%, "though bookings trends continued to moderate," Hood said.
* Frontier and support services: $2.11bn, up 4%.

Microsoft Cloud revenue, the combination of Azure, Microsoft 365 commercial cloud and Industry solutions cloud, was $63.9bn, up 30%. Its gross margin fell to 66% from 68% a year earlier.

Commercial bookings fell 12%, a decline Hood tied to "large Azure commitments in the prior year." Bookings had grown 112% and 230% in the first two quarters of fiscal 2026, according to Microsoft's metrics spreadsheet. Commercial remaining performance obligation, the contracted revenue not yet recognized, stood at $677bn, up 73% on the year but flat on the $678bn reported in June. About 30% of it is expected to be recognized within 12 months. Hood warned that "timing related to significant Azure commitments like these will result in material volatility in bookings, making quarterly growth rates less indicative of underlying sales execution."

### Devices and Consumer

The consumer segment shrank. Revenue fell 3% to $15.48bn, although operating income rose 2% to $5.36bn, lifting the margin to 35% from 33%. Lower amortization of intangible assets from the Activision Blizzard acquisition did most of that work.

Windows OEM and devices revenue fell 22%, or $1.0bn, to $3.55bn. Windows OEM revenue alone dropped 27%. Hood listed three causes: the prior year's demand from the end of Windows 10 support, "inventory drawdowns by OEM and channel partners, and weaker PC market demand." She added: "Inventory levels remain elevated."

Xbox revenue declined 2% to $5.38bn. Content and services fell 2% on weaker third-party content and Xbox Game Pass, and hardware fell 14% on lower console volumes. Nadella said Minecraft had a record quarter and pointed to Modern Warfare 4, launched the week before the call, and Grand Theft Auto VI, "which is coming to XBOX next month."

## OpenAI: $10bn of revenue and a 24% stake

The most consequential disclosure for anyone gauging Microsoft's dependence on one customer sits in the notes to the 10-Q. "For the three months ended September 30, 2026, we recorded revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, inclusive of revenue-sharing payments, of $10.0 billion," the filing states. Accounts receivable from OpenAI rose to $7.2bn at September 30 from $6.0bn at June 30.

That is 10.8% of quarterly revenue, by PPC Land's calculation. Gabriela Borges of Goldman Sachs put it at 11% on the call and asked how Microsoft sees the balance between OpenAI's models and its own. Microsoft makes the disclosure because OpenAI is an equity-method investee and therefore a related party under US accounting rules.

The filing puts Microsoft's interest at "an approximate 24% interest on an as-converted basis." When the companies restructured their partnership in October 2025, PPC Land reported a stake of [roughly 27% on an as-converted diluted basis](https://ppc.land/microsoft-and-openai-restructure-partnership-with-new-governance-framework/), valued then at about $135bn. The two descriptions are not on an identical basis, and the 10-Q does not explain the difference. Microsoft has made funding commitments of $13.0bn, of which $12.0bn had been paid by September 30. The April 2026 amendment that made Microsoft's IP license non-exclusive and let OpenAI use other clouds [left OpenAI's revenue-share payments to Microsoft in place through 2030, subject to a cap](https://ppc.land/microsoft-and-openai-rewrite-the-deal-what-actually-changed/). The 10-Q repeats that Microsoft "will continue to receive revenue-sharing payments."

On the income statement OpenAI barely registered this time. Microsoft recorded $272m of net gains from its OpenAI investments in other income, against $4.1bn of losses a year earlier. After tax the gain added $207m, or $0.03 a share, to net income.

Nadella, answering Borges, described OpenAI's latest models as part of a menu rather than a dependency. "They were fantastic models, and we're obviously very thrilled about the progress OpenAI has made with Astra and also what's to come," he said, before describing how customers move between frontier models, open-weight models and Microsoft's own MAI models. "It's like I may start at the frontier. I may go to an open weight. I may go to an MAI model. I may go back to the frontier for the next drop for a few months, come out."

Earlier in the call he set a target for those in-house models: "delivering capabilities comparable to leading models within three to six months of their release at a fraction of the training cost." Microsoft has finished pre-training a base model called MAI-Base-2, which Nadella said has "4 to 12 times greater training compute efficiency" than other open-weight models Microsoft tested. A coding model, MAI Code Flash, "had 3 million users in GitHub Copilot last month alone."

## Capex, cash and $364.6bn of leases

Capital expenditures, including assets acquired under finance leases, rose 30% to $45.2bn. Cash paid for property and equipment more than doubled, up 103% to $39.4bn. Hood said spending fell short of plan because of third-party delays. "Capital expenditures were $45.2 billion, as some third-party capacity deliveries we expected in Q1 were delayed," she said. Roughly three quarters of the total went to short-lived assets, mainly CPUs and GPUs, against about half a year earlier, according to the slides.

The delays pushed the annual figure down. "In Q2, we expect CapEx spend will be over $50 billion. Therefore, for the calendar year, spend should be approximately $170 billion due to the 3P capacity delays noted earlier," Hood said. In July, Microsoft had put [calendar 2026 capital expenditure at approximately $175bn](https://ppc.land/microsoft-search-ad-growth-drops-to-10-as-azure-tops-100-billion/), including the effect of a lease reclassification. Spending in the three quarters of calendar 2026 already reported totals $118.1bn, which leaves about $51.9bn for October to December, by PPC Land's calculation. Hood expects spending to accelerate again in the second half of the fiscal year, from January to June 2027, as the delayed deliveries arrive.

[Free cash flow](https://ppc.land/free-cash-flow/) fell 27% to $18.63bn, from $25.66bn. Operating cash flow rose 29% to $58.0bn on "strong cloud billings and collections," but additions to property and equipment rose to $39.37bn from $19.39bn. Cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments dropped $12.3bn in three months, to $64.5bn. Microsoft also repaid $4.85bn of debt.

We will post our prepared remarks to our website immediately following the call until the complete transcript is available.

You can replay the call and view the transcript on the Microsoft Investor Relations website. During this call, we will be making forward-looking statements, which are predictions, projections, and assumptions. Or other statements about future events. **Satya Nadella** — *Chairman and Chief Executive Officer*

Thank you very much, Jonathan. It was a fast start to our fiscal year. Microsoft Cloud revenue surpassed $63 billion with growth accelerating to 30% year over year. We are focused on 3 things: designing AI to empower people, ensuring every organization has sovereignty over its own learning, and building trust with controls that ensure agency safety and security. Now let’s talk about how we are making progress on those goals as we build a new tech stack, starting with Copilot. We announced our biggest update to Copilot to date this quarter, bringing together Chat, Cowork, Autopilot, and Code into one unified experience.

It’s one product experience across commercial and consumer and comes with all of Office built in. We think of Copilot as the new OS for work. Customers are increasingly turning to Copilot to get real work done. Automated tasks has nearly doubled since July. Daily users are up nearly 50% quarter over quarter and over 5x year over year. User satisfaction improved nearly 20% quarter over quarter to another all-time high, and 90% of Copilot queries use auto mode, which dynamically routes tasks across models optimizing for quality, speed, and cost.

These improvements are translating into larger purchases. The number of customers with more than 50,000 Copilot seats increased over 8x year over year, including Capgemini, HCL Tech, Hitachi Group, Truist Financial, and UK Revenue and Customs Department. And just last week, Volkswagen announced plans to deploy Copilot to more than 330,000 employees, one of the largest deployments to date in Europe. We’re also seeing strong momentum with E7, which brings together Copilot, E5, Entra, and agent 365.

Thousands of customers in every industry have purchased the suite to date, including Amadeus, BlackRock, Fiserv, and New South Wales Health Department and ZEISS. Our business model is expanding from per-seat subscriptions to include consumption, expanding our TAM and ARPU. The subscription brings increasingly capable everyday intelligence to every user. Typically, IT funds this, consolidating frontier advances for everyone across the organization. And as agents take on higher-value work, consumption opens up business-funded demand with spending tied directly to the value these agents deliver.

The number of Copilot customers actively consuming credits through usage-based billing grew over 75% over the quarter. When it comes to software development, all major coding agents have shown up to work on GitHub. Agent-generated PRs have increased 6x over the past 6 months, and agents now open more than a third of all PRs on the platform. We are very hard at work on reliability as agentic activity on GitHub soars. At GitHub Universe this morning, we shared how we are expanding capacity and rebuilding the core Git architecture for the agentic wave.

Also at Universe, we announced broad availability of Copilot Fusion, which is all about bringing multi-model orchestration to software development. It delivers frontier-level quality up to 40% faster and at up to 77% lower costs. Credit consumption from agentic features on GitHub has more than doubled since usage-based billing went into effect. And we’re also helping developers secure their code and turn AI-generated code into high-quality software. GitHub Advanced Security revenue increased over 50% year over year as customers use its AI capabilities to scan entire repos and fix vulnerabilities in real time.

In the business application space, we are extending this vision of Copilot as the new OS for work, bringing the business logic and capabilities of Dynamics 365 directly into Copilot and helping every organization stand up their own infinite SaaS factory. This quarter, we introduced 30 new Copilot skills across Dynamics 365, which enables customers to access CRM and ERP capabilities directly in the flow of work. In recruiting, more than 10 million LinkedIn members use our LinkedIn AI-powered job search daily, and 25,000 customers are using our agentic hiring solutions.

Recruiters using Hiring Assistant are finding interview-quality applicants 33% faster while reviewing 83% fewer profiles to find qualified match. In healthcare, we automated 30 million patient encounters this quarter, up 70% year over year, helping clinicians spend less time on administrative work and more time with patients. 10 providers, including Advocate Health, Mass General Brigham, Mercy, Intermountain Health, and others, have used our solutions to document over million encounters each since the beginning of the calendar year.

And in science, our FDE teams are working with customers to use discovery to accelerate scientific progress. A great example is Saint-Gobain, which used discovery to accelerate the development of low-carbon construction materials. Underneath our first-party agentic experience is a common platform. It starts with Foundry, which is becoming an increasingly important driver of our growth. Foundry helps organizations build learning loops grounded in their business context and deploy agents safely at scale.

We now have over 120,000 Foundry customers with revenue more than tripling year over year. Foundry’s model choice and feature set coupled with its deep integration across our stack is driving differentiation. Azure OpenAI directly benefited in the last quarter with big advances in OpenAI models. And when you couple this with our model choice built into Foundry, customers are able to build solutions optimizing across quality, cost, and performance. In fact, the number of customers building agentic solutions with multiple models increased 5x year over year, and revenue from open-source models on Foundry increased 10x.

We also continue to make rapid progress with our first-party models. Our goal is to advance the cost-to-outcome frontier, which means delivering capabilities comparable to leading models within 3 to 6 months of their release at a fraction of the training cost, thereby allowing us to transfer those cost benefits to customers. And you see this in our products today. MAI Cyber now powers over 40% of the scans in our Agentic M-Code Scanner at 18% lower cost per scan. MAI Transcribe is the most accurate and cheapest transcription model in the world, supporting Dragon Copilot’s multilingual workflow.

MAI CodeFlash has 3 million users in GitHub Copilot last month alone, helping developers get more out of their AI credits. Microsoft Decision One is our new model for structured decision-making, outperforming both LLMs and other decision models in latency and quality. Over 4,000 customers, including Atos Group, Equinor, and RBI, have already used it in the first month since its release. And we recently completed pre-training MAI Base 2, which outperforms other open-weight models we tested with 4 to 12 times greater training compute efficiency.

This base model will be used in the upcoming MAI models across thinking, code, and science. Beyond models, we are making the harness behind our own Copilot experience available to customers in Foundry. It gives customers a Microsoft-managed way to build agents that reason, use tools, complete complex long-running work while preserving their choice of model. Another critical layer is data. We now have 44,000 paid Fabric customers, up more than 50% year over year. We are bringing Foundry and Fabric closer together so you can build build your own agents right next to data.

Over 19,000 customers now use Foundry and Fabric as enterprises connect and operate agents over real-time operational, analytical, and unstructured data. Customers are also rapidly deploying our AI-optimized databases, including PostgreSQL, SQL DB Hyperscale, Cosmos DB, to give agents fast, secure access to the data and context they need PostgreSQL growth accelerated for the 4th consecutive quarter, and the number of PostgreSQL customers also using Foundry accelerated to 90% year over year. We also have one of the most important databases for any enterprise, which is the knowledge underneath Microsoft 365 spanning people, their relationships, documents, emails, meetings, chats, projects, and other artifacts.

WorkIQ makes this context available to every agentic workload, and with Microsoft IQ, we are bringing together WorkIQ, FabricIQ, and FoundryIQ as a unified context for agentic systems. Nearly 60,000 customers are accessing context across Microsoft IQ, up 25% quarter over quarter. As enterprises deploy more agents, they also need to govern them at scale. With Agent 365, we provide a platform for AI observability, enabling customers to manage, secure, and optimize the performance and cost of their agents Over 50 million agents are now in the registry, up over 30% quarter over quarter.

And finally, as agents gain greater access to enterprise data and systems, security becomes even more critical. Our approach is to separate intelligence from authority, enforcing identity, permissions, monitoring, and containment outside the model itself. Last week, we expanded Perception with new capabilities to help customers secure and contain agentic insiders, including expanded agent discovery across local and cloud environments, dynamic permissions that enforce least privileged access for each task, and continuous risk assessment.

We also introduced teams of guardian agents that continuously monitor agent activity to help prevent unsafe actions before they occur. And we are seeing encouraging feedback on perception overall from preview customers, including KPMG, Nationwide Building Society, Northern Trust, Celentis. More broadly, we are helping customers secure and govern AI use across the enterprise. Customers have used Microsoft Purview to audit over 7.6 billion agent activities to date, up 5x quarter over quarter. Underlying everything I’ve talked about so far is our infrastructure.

We are building against a growing book of business with a fungible fleet that allows us to dynamically allocate capacity to the highest value opportunities across compute, data, foundry, and copilot. Accelerating demand led to us adding 24 new data centers across 5 continents this quarter. And we are bringing capacity online faster, reducing dock-to-live times by about 20% quarter over quarter for new GB300s in our biggest regions, which make up the majority of the GPU deployments. At the same time, we continue to get more from the infrastructure we already have have by optimizing across the data center design, silicon systems, software, and models.

For example, we increased the throughput for Copilot workloads by over 50% quarter over quarter. We continue to scale our fleet with the latest innovations from NVIDIA, AMD, alongside our own Maya systems. We have docked our first NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs and are very excited about it. Maya 200 is already delivering up to 1.7 times more tokens per watt across the AI experience in Teams and Copilot, and Maya 300 will drive further gains, delivering 40% more tokens per watt compared to leading GPU-based systems.

Our growth extends beyond GPUs. We continue to see strong adoption of our cloud-native Cobalt CPUs, improving price performance for general-purpose cloud workloads. All-up Azure growth was broad-based across both enterprises and small and medium business segments and spanning both core cloud services and AI infrastructure. Finally, let me turn to devices and consumer. In Windows, we are executing on our vision to bring hybrid intelligence to every desk and every home, making every PC a secure agent box.

As more capable models run locally, we see an opportunity to make more intelligence effectively unmeted. We are working with the broader hardware ecosystem to bring these capabilities to a new generation of PCs across AMD’s Ryzen AI 400 Series, Intel Core Ultra Series 3, Qualcomm Snapdragon X8 Gen 3, X2 series. And earlier this month, we also announced new PCs powered by NVIDIA’s RTX Spark and DGX Station for Windows. With these new devices, you can run last year’s Frontier models on your laptop and last quarter’s model at your desk.

# Microsoft Q1: Copilot Usage Jumps, Seat Count Goes Missing

Microsoft grew Q1 revenue 19% to $92.3 billion but gave no update on its paid Copilot seat count, leading with usage instead. As it pushes E7 and leans harder on usage-based billing for AI, IT buyers face harder-to-forecast spend and fresh leverage at renewal.

![](/api/portrait/fdef044e-23d1-4066-ac73-a741a3ccf00a/avatar-r2-h6a5626b7-5288-460f-81c8-5b43ed972f1e-1792572438878-dc063ea7.jpg)[Marcus Law](/author/marcus-law)

![](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.uctoday.com%2Farticle-images%2F1793268229479-microsoft-q1-fy27-featured.jpg&w=3840&q=75)![Red-brick Microsoft office building with the Microsoft logo and wordmark on its facade, a rooftop terrace with seating, plants and people, and glass towers behind](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.uctoday.com%2Farticle-images%2F1793268229479-microsoft-q1-fy27-featured.jpg&w=3840&q=75)

Microsoft's Atlanta office. Image: Microsoft

For two years, investors and IT buyers have asked Microsoft the same thing about Copilot: are people paying for it, and are they using it? For the past three quarters the answer has come with a number attached. This quarter it didn't.

Microsoft's [first-quarter fiscal 2027 results](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/Investor/earnings/FY-2027-Q1/press-release-webcast), for the three months to September 30, were strong. Revenue rose 19% to $92.3 billion and Microsoft Cloud revenue grew 30% to $63.9 billion. Yet the figure that has become the industry's barometer for workplace AI, paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats, was missing from both the release and the call. In its place came usage growth, consumption credits and a new top-tier license.

That is more than a change in what Microsoft reports. The company is [moving the measure of its AI business from seats to usage](https://cxtoday.com/from-saas-to-agents-as-a-service-microsofts-q4-earnings-redefine-the-cx-tech-stack), and the way it bills customers is moving with it. For buyers, that means an AI bill that is harder to forecast. Yet the same results suggest customers have more leverage at renewal than the headline growth implies.

## A strong quarter, minus one number

On most measures, Microsoft had little to hide. Operating income rose 21% to $45.9 billion. Commercial remaining performance obligation, the contracted revenue Microsoft has yet to recognize, rose 73% to $677 billion. Shares rose 4% in extended trading, [CNBC reported](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/28/microsoft-msft-q1-earnings-report-2027.html).

CNBC also noted that the company "did not disclose the number of paid seats." When an analyst pressed the point on the call, CFO Amy Hood didn't dodge it. "We did not disclose, to answer your direct question, an update on the Copilot number this quarter. We talked about momentum in revenue and usage," [she said](https://aka.ms/transcriptfy27q1).

## Why the missing number matters

The seat count has been the yardstick because Microsoft made it one. When the company first disclosed 15 million paid seats in January, J.P. Gownder, vice president and principal analyst at Forrester, called it "disappointing uptake of the tool," [Computerworld reported](https://www.computerworld.com/article/4124591/microsoft-touts-m365-copilot-momentum-claims-15m-paid-users.html).

Microsoft answered the doubters quarter by quarter. It reported [more than 20 million](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/investor/events/fy-2026/earnings-fy-2026-q3) in April and, in its [Q4 FY26 results](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/investor/earnings/fy-2026-q4/press-release-webcast), "over 30 million paid seats," double January's figure and a milestone [we reported in July](https://uctoday.com/microsoft-365-copilot-passes-30-million-paid-seats-as-cloud-and-ai-growth-power-record-quarter). Having built the benchmark, Microsoft has now stopped updating it, so there is no way to tell whether paid adoption kept pace.

The timing is awkward. Alphabet reported the same day, and Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian put a number on it. "Across all our AI services, we have sold more than 100 million seats for knowledge work," [he told analysts](https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/10/29/alphabet-googl-q3-2026-earnings-call-transcript/).

What Microsoft offered instead was usage. Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella described Copilot as "one product experience across commercial and consumer," and said: "Daily users are up nearly 50 percent quarter over quarter, and over 5X year over year." Automated tasks, he said, "have nearly doubled since July."

Those are big multiples, but Microsoft gave no base for them, nor said whether the daily-user figure counts business users alone. They tell buyers that Copilot is being used more, not how many organizations are paying for it.

The deployment signals were more concrete. Nadella said the number of customers with more than 50,000 Copilot seats "increased over 8X year over year." Volkswagen, he added, plans to deploy Copilot to more than 330,000 employees, "one of the largest deployments to date in Europe."

## Underneath it: from seats to meters

The reason for the shift became clear when Nadella explained how Microsoft now makes money from AI. "Our business model is expanding from per-seat subscriptions to include consumption, expanding our TAM and ARPU," he told analysts.

He described two funding streams. The subscription brings everyday AI to every user, and "typically, IT funds this." Then, "as agents take on higher-value work, consumption opens up business-funded demand, with spending tied directly to the value these agents deliver." That second stream is already growing fast: the number of Copilot customers "actively consuming credits through usage-based billing grew over 75 percent over the quarter."

Seen that way, a seat count captures only half the business, and increasingly the less dynamic half.

The seat half is being pushed upmarket. E7, the suite that combines Copilot, E5, Entra and Agent 365, went on sale on May 1, and UC Today covered [the launch of Microsoft's $99 E7 tier](https://uctoday.com/microsoft-launches-99-m365-e7-tier-and-agent-365-to-tame-ai-sprawl) in March. Nadella said "thousands of customers" have bought it, and Hood said E7 "has already reached millions of paid seats."

The seat price is only the start, though. In a June [analysis for Directions on Microsoft](https://www.directionsonmicrosoft.com/understanding-m365-e7-the-three-risks-behind-the-99-price-point/), licensing adviser Lane Shelton wrote that "the $99 number, on its own, is only the down payment on the total investment required to operate E7 at scale." Consumption meters such as Copilot Studio credits, he noted, are not included in E7.

Further down the market, pay-as-you-go is becoming the default rather than an option. In a [Partner Center announcement](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/partner-center/announcements/2026-october), Microsoft says usage-based billing will be on by default for new Microsoft 365 Copilot Business licenses bought through CSP from December 1, 2026. The default spending limit is 4,000 Copilot Credits per user per month, which admins can adjust. The change will initially not be available in 11 markets, including France and Germany, though the UK is not among them.

That push upmarket is happening while the core of the business softens. Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue grew 18% on an adjusted basis (17% reported), but Hood said strength in GitHub Copilot was "partially offset by weaker sales execution in our M365 E3 and standalone SKUs." Paid M365 commercial seats grew 5%, mainly in small business and frontline worker offerings. She said Microsoft continues "to evolve our sales motions to balance those more traditional SKU per-seat rhythms with the newer premium E7, M365 Copilot, and usage-based productivity offerings."

Microsoft is reshaping its workforce at the same time. It has launched a [voluntary exit offer](https://blogs.microsoft.com/blog/2026/10/26/introducing-a-voluntary-exit-offer/) for [eligible employees in participating teams](https://uctoday.com/microsoft-opens-voluntary-exits-to-copilot-and-ai-teams) in Canada, India, the UK and the US, and its post gives no headcount. [CNBC reported](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/26/microsoft-msft-voluntary-buyouts.html) that "around 60,000 Microsoft employees are eligible," citing a person familiar with the matter. It also noted that Microsoft announced 4,800 layoffs in July. Hood said Q2 cost guidance includes an estimate for the exit offer.

New reporting makes the trend harder to read. Microsoft now has two segments: Agents and Infra, which brought in $76.8 billion, up 25%, and Devices and Consumer, which fell 3% to $15.5 billion.

Behind all of this sits a huge infrastructure bill. Azure grew 48%, and Hood said "customer demand continues to exceed available supply." Capital expenditure was $45.2 billion. She expects Q2 capex to "be over $50 billion" and calendar-year spend to be "approximately $170 billion."

## What it means for buyers

For IT and UC buyers, AI spend is splitting into two lines. One is a predictable seat license, increasingly E7, that IT owns. The other is a variable agent bill that business units can run up themselves. It is far harder to forecast and, from December, on by default for new Copilot Business licenses sold through CSP.

Even Microsoft acknowledges the risk of getting that mix wrong. "We don't want them to overbuy one thing and then feel like they're token maxing because that doesn't serve anybody's purpose," Nadella said. Hood was candid about how quickly the model will spread, saying "it will be a slower move outside of coding," though she still sees "encouraging signs."

That gives buyers a stronger hand than the 19% growth rate implies. Microsoft has no updated seat number to cite, it has admitted weaker E3 execution, and it is still reworking its sales motions. Customers being asked to move from E3 or E5 to E7 are negotiating with a supplier that has a lot riding on that move.

## What to watch next

* **Ignite, November 17–20.** [Microsoft's San Francisco conference](https://uctoday.com/events/ignite-2026) is the likely stage for more Copilot pricing and packaging news. Listen for whether a seat figure returns.
* **CSP billing from December 1.** Copilot Business customers buying through partners should check the default 4,000-credit limit before it applies, and decide who owns the meter.

* **Q2 guidance.** Microsoft expects revenue of $96 billion to $97.1 billion and M365 commercial cloud growth of about 19% in constant currency, with "some improvement in execution across E3 and our standalone SKUs." If E3 doesn't recover, the pressure on Microsoft's sales teams grows.
* **Renewal clauses.** Before signing for E7, ask for spending caps on consumption meters, price protection on credits, and the right to move users between tiers. The seat price can be fixed up front. As Shelton's analysis warns, the meters on top of it are much harder to predict.

Until Microsoft puts a seat number back on the table, buyers should read the usage multiples as a sales pitch rather than a forecast, and budget for the meter as carefully as for the license.

## FAQs

### Did Microsoft report its paid Copilot seat count for Q1 FY27?

No. CFO Amy Hood told analysts Microsoft did not disclose an update on the Copilot number this quarter and talked instead about momentum in revenue and usage. The last figure, in Microsoft's Q4 FY26 results in July, was over 30 million paid seats.

### What changes for Microsoft 365 Copilot Business billing on December 1, 2026?

Usage-based billing will be on by default for new Microsoft 365 Copilot Business licenses bought through CSP, with a default limit of 4,000 Copilot Credits per user per month that admins can adjust. It will initially not be available in 11 markets, including France and Germany, but the UK is not among them.

### Does the $99 Microsoft 365 E7 price cover all AI costs?

Not on its own. E7 combines Copilot, E5, Entra and Agent 365, but Directions on Microsoft's Lane Shelton notes that consumption meters such as Copilot Studio credits are not included. Before signing, buyers should ask for spending caps on meters, price protection on credits and the right to move users between tiers.

# Microsoft (MSFT) Stock Shrugs Off Q1 Earnings As AI Spending Looms

Sasha Jovanovic

Microsoft stock barely moved today, slipping 0.2% to about US$530 after a year where the shares climbed strongly and traders had already priced in big expectations. The latest Q1 FY27 earnings drop was anything but sleepy. Revenue reached US$92.3b and basic earnings per share came in at US$4.93, both backed by a powerful cloud and artificial intelligence engine.

In the short term, that muted price reaction can look underwhelming. Over a longer horizon, the focus shifts to the gap between a 27.6x P/E and a valuation case that still leans on aggressive AI buildout and heavy capital spending.

Love the sheer scale of Microsoft's US$92.3b quarter and US$4.93 in earnings per share, but uneasy about paying a 27.6x P/E multiple tied to heavy AI spending and capex commitments? Compare that profile with companies filtered for stronger balance sheets and disciplined fundamentals in our [list of solid balance sheet and fundamentals stocks (23 results)](https://simplywall.st/discover/investing-ideas/10146/solid-balance-sheet-and-fundamentals/us?utm_medium=finance_user&utm_campaign=cta_screener_solid_balance_sheet&utm_source=yahoo&blueprint=4822056).

## Q1 2027 Earnings Summary

* **Revenue (Q1 2027 vs. Q1 2026):** US$92.3b vs. US$77.7b (up about 19%)
* **Net Income (Excl. Extra Items, Q1 2027 vs. Q1 2026):** US$36.6b vs. US$27.7b (up about 32%)
* **Basic EPS (Q1 2027 vs. Q1 2026):** US$4.93 vs. US$3.73 (up about 32%)

* **Operating Margin (Q1 2027):** approximately 50% (a slight improvement compared with the prior-year period)

Microsoft is pouring an unprecedented $170B into AI buildout. ## Microsoft's AI Ambitions Confront Hard Utilisation Tests

For the bullish story to hold, Microsoft needs its AI and cloud build to translate into durable, higher quality earnings power.

> *"Company scale in AI infrastructure, with over two thirds of US$31.9b quarterly CapEx going into short-lived CPUs and GPUs and a plan to invest roughly US$190b in capital expenditures for calendar 2026, is aimed at supporting higher cloud and AI consumption that can lift revenue and spread fixed costs across a larger base to support margins."*

Free cash flow stayed positive, supported by bond market access and workforce reshaping. Together these factors point to infrastructure scale-up without immediate margin breakage.

## Microsoft AI Buildout: Margins Hold, Cash Strain Shows

Bearish investors worry that Microsoft's AI build turns into a margin drag rather than an earnings engine.

> *"Although demand for AI infrastructure is currently described as exceeding supply, the heavy reliance on short-lived GPU and CPU assets and very high capital expenditures could compress gross margin percentage for Microsoft Cloud if efficiency gains or AI usage patterns do not keep pace."*

Q1 does not show that compression yet. Microsoft Cloud gross margin sits near 66% and company operating margin is about 50%. The miss is on a different milestone. Capex of roughly US$45.2b and planned calendar 2026 spend of around US$170b to US$190b already outstrip free cash flow, which came in at US$18.6b.

# Microsoft's Azure Guidance Clears the Bar as Capex Bill Tops $50 Billion

![Microsofts, Azure, Guidance, Clears, Bar, Capex, Bill, Tops, Billion, Microsoft Illustration mit AI erstellt.](https://mdb.ad-hoc-news.de/bild/bild-2671697_1200_0.webp)

Microsoft delivered a first fiscal quarter for 2027 that beat expectations on both revenue and profit, then followed it with guidance that cleared analyst forecasts as well. The results, released yesterday, showed revenue of $92.3 billion, up 19% year over year, while diluted GAAP earnings per share climbed 32% to $4.92. Operating income came in at $45.9 billion.

The beat wasn't confined to adjusted figures — GAAP profit rose sharply too, a sign the quarter's strength rests on more than a single non-standard metric. Investors responded positively, with the stock up 1.4% in pre-market trading today.

## Cloud momentum carries the quarter

Microsoft Cloud generated $63.9 billion in revenue, a 30% increase, and Azure revenue jumped 48%. The company expects that momentum to hold. For the second fiscal quarter of 2027, it guided to Azure growth of 49% to 50% at constant currency — above what analysts had penciled in, according to Reuters. Total revenue for the period is forecast at $96.0 billion to $97.1 billion, a range that also topped consensus estimates.

The guidance matters because it signals no imminent cooling in the cloud business. One caveat deserves attention: Microsoft states the forward Azure figure explicitly on a constant-currency basis, so the comparison with the quarter just reported isn't apples to apples.

## Oppenheimer raises its target

Ahead of the release, Oppenheimer analyst Brian Schwartz lifted his price target on Microsoft to $625 from $570 on Monday, keeping his positive rating. He pointed to enterprise customer demand underpinning both Azure and Microsoft 365. The upgrade is an analyst view and doesn't pre-empt the reported results — but it does shift the focus onto the operating business rather than headline AI announcements.

The stock had gained 3.3% earlier in the week ahead of the print, helped by a friendlier climate for AI names as Reuters reported renewed optimism before earnings from Microsoft and other major cloud providers. No single company announcement explained that move.

## The other side of the ledger

Against the growth story sits a hefty spending bill. Microsoft expects capital expenditures above $50 billion in the second fiscal quarter, and around $170 billion in total for calendar 2026. The company's infrastructure ambitions are concrete: on October 12 it unveiled Maia 300, its next AI inference platform, and said it would expand Azure Maia capacity into the multi-gigawatt range from 2027. That is a plan, not capacity already in place.

Microsoft is also working the cost side. Reuters reported Monday that the company is using voluntary severance offers to contain expenses and help fund AI investments. Microsoft confirmed a time-limited offer including financial support and career-planning assistance. According to AP, it extends to roughly 60,000 employees, or about 27% of the global workforce — a figure describing who is eligible, not a fixed layoff target. Microsoft gave no expected take-up, so no specific savings figure can be derived from the program.

For investors, the two signals belong together: demand is strong and the outlook beats expectations, but converting that growth into returns requires heavy outlays. Cloud revenue trends and capital discipline will be judged in tandem — robust demand on its own doesn't answer the question of what the capital ultimately earns.

# Microsoft’s Free Cash Flow Beats Forecasts Despite Massive AI Spending

Microsoft generated $18.6 billion in free cash flow in July–September 2026 as stronger cloud collections helped fund AI infrastructure and some spending shifted to later quarters.

[![Markus Kasanmascheff](data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB2aWV3Qm94PSIwIDAgOTYgOTYiIHdpZHRoPSI5NiIgaGVpZ2h0PSI5NiIgeG1sbnM9Imh0dHA6Ly93d3cudzMub3JnLzIwMDAvc3ZnIj48L3N2Zz4=)](https://winbuzzer.com/author/markus/ "Markus Kasanmascheff")

By [Markus Kasanmascheff](https://winbuzzer.com/author/markus/)

![Microsoft Datacenters Infrastructure Servers AI](https://cdn-chilj.nitrocdn.com/gYFaTcLxknXlucWgXPjHDdhAuyobJjHx/assets/images/optimized/rev-a633932/winbuzzer.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Microsoft-Datacenters-Infrastructure-Servers-AI-1068x610-1067x.jpg "Microsoft Datacenters Infrastructure Servers AI")

TL;DR

* Cash Generation: Microsoft generated $18.6 billion after cash capital spending in its September quarter, roughly $10 billion above analyst expectations.
* Cloud Growth: Azure cloud revenue rose 48% year over year to $33.2 billion as Microsoft sold more services from existing computing capacity.
* Delayed Deliveries: Some infrastructure spending shifted into later quarters; Microsoft expects capital expenditure above $50 billion in its fiscal second quarter.
* Profit Growth: Net income rose 32% year over year, while growth excluding OpenAI investment effects was 18%.

Microsoft generated $18.6 billion in free cash flow in the quarter ended September 30, 2026, as cash from operations exceeded payments for property and equipment despite those payments roughly doubling from a year earlier. Stronger cloud collections helped fund its AI infrastructure buildout, while delayed capacity deliveries pushed some spending into later quarters.

The software and cloud company’s [fiscal 2027 first-quarter revenue reached $92.3 billion](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/investor/earnings/fy-2027-q1/press-release-webcast), up 19% from a year earlier. Operating income increased 21% to $45.9 billion. Microsoft released the results October 28.

The free cash flow figure was [about $10 billion above analyst expectations](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/business/microsofts-cloud-growth-cash-flow-offer-respite-ai-spending-fears-6501191), Reuters reported. Shares rose more than 5% in after-hours trading following a second-quarter sales and cloud-growth outlook that also exceeded estimates.

## **Turning Existing Capacity Into Sales**

Azure, Microsoft’s cloud platform for running customer applications and AI workloads, produced $33.2 billion in quarterly revenue. Its 48% year-over-year growth rate accelerated from [42% in the preceding quarter](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/investor/earnings/fy-2027-q1/metrics), using Microsoft’s recast comparison figures.

Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood attributed the stronger performance partly to getting more saleable capacity from existing hardware. Engineering improvements freed capacity on graphics processors, or GPUs, for additional customers. Work on general-purpose processors, or CPUs, also let Microsoft sell capacity that had previously been underused.

Hood said revenue from Foundry, the platform developers use to build AI systems, more than tripled from a year earlier. Alongside the extra GPU capacity, Microsoft benefited from higher revenue per token, the units processed by AI models. That gave the company two ways to increase sales: serving more demand with installed hardware and collecting more revenue for the model usage it supplied.

The broader Microsoft Cloud measure reached $63.9 billion, up 30% year over year. That includes business software as well as Azure: Microsoft 365 cloud, its subscription productivity software business, generated $27.8 billion. The company had [first passed $50 billion in quarterly cloud revenue](https://winbuzz
